answer:
1. The animation compares buying and renting using US history from January 1991 on. Each tile is one possible starting month, 247 in all. A lit tile means the buyer came out ahead and a dark tile means the renter did. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The animation labels itself "ILLUSTRATIVE" and says "US only · history, not a forecast." A final scene follows a character named Nina, who is deciding between an apartment and a house.

2. The holding period changes. In frame 1, every one of the 247 start months is lit for a 15-year hold, and the label says "every one (100%)." Frame 2 adds that the weakest case still left the buyer $79,829 ahead. Frame 3 switches to "held ten years," and a band of tiles in the middle goes dark, so for those start months the renter was ahead. Frame 4 returns to "held fifteen years" with all tiles lit again. Frames 5 and 6 move to Nina's story. Her stay length is labeled "unknown," and "the rent tag" on the apartment stays "unchanged."

3. Over 15-year holds, buying beat renting in every historical start month. Over 10-year holds, buying won in most months but lost in some. The result depends on how long you stay. Nina's case shows that her own stay is unknown, so the history doesn't guarantee an outcome for her.

4. A viewer would probably take away that buying has historically paid off if they stay a long time, around 15 years. The payoff is less certain over 10 years, and nobody can know their own stay in advance. The advice is conditional: buying looks better the longer you expect to stay.

5. This is partly my own reading. The animation shows the 100% result at 15 years, the dark tiles at 10 years, the "unknown" stay length and the "history, not a forecast" disclaimer. It never says "you should buy" or "you should rent." The advice to buy only if you expect a long stay is my inference from those visuals. The animation also doesn't show the cost inputs from your question, such as interest, tax, insurance and repairs, so I can't tell whether it counted them.
